Africa pushes for local processing
The programme comes as African governments increasingly seek to capture more value from their natural resources.
Zambia is Africa’s second-largest copper producer, Zimbabwe is the continent’s leading lithium supplier, Guinea is the world’s largest bauxite producer and Madagascar holds deposits of cobalt, graphite and nickel. Nigeria’s mineral resources remain largely untapped. Indonesia is the world’s largest nickel producer.
Zimbabwe is already pushing lithium producers to process the mineral locally and plans to ban exports of unprocessed lithium ore. The country has also suspended exports of tungsten and antimony.
Kenya is similarly planning to restrict exports of unprocessed minerals and build refineries to increase local processing.
The UN expects demand for critical minerals to rise sharply as countries expand renewable energy and electric-vehicle production, increasing pressure on resource-rich nations to capture more of the economic value generated by their mineral wealth.

articles.title: Are Lynas Rare Earths Gaining From China's Curbs (ASX:LYC)? - Kalkine Media
articles.summary: Are Lynas Rare Earths Gaining From China's Curbs (ASX:LYC)?  Kalkine Media
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- China has tightened enforcement of critical mineral export controls, adding reporting and anti-circumvention rules.
- Lynas remains the largest producer of separated rare earths outside China as it searches for a new leader.
- The company confirmed earlier this month that takeover talks conducted earlier in the year did not proceed.
Lynas Rare Earths (ASX:LYC) Basic Materials Lynas Rare EARTHS Ltd (ASX:LYC) 13.71 AUD +0.065 0.477% Last Updated at: 2026-09-30T05:10:00Z remains a focal point for the Australian market today as China tightens enforcement of its critical mineral export controls, a shift that reinforces the strategic weight of the largest rare earths producer outside China at a time when the company is also searching for a new leader and has confirmed that takeover talks earlier in the year did not proceed.
China's tighter enforcement
Beijing has introduced new mechanisms to identify violations of its export control regime and to prevent circumvention. A reporting framework that took effect in July targets breaches involving strategic mineral dual-use items, including exports without licences and shipments outside approved conditions.
The rules explicitly cover attempts to get around controls by modifying or splitting products into components. Authorities may reward verified reports of violations, while companies that self-report may have that considered when penalties are set.
Separately, China's Ministry of Commerce has gained authority to investigate foreign measures it considers harmful to Chinese supply-chain security, adding another policy lever that can affect trade in strategic minerals. Taken together, the measures suggest Beijing intends to treat critical mineral exports as a closely monitored strategic supply chain rather than an ordinary commodity trade.
What it means for non-China supply
The practical effect is to raise compliance risk for anyone relying on Chinese-origin rare earths. Manufacturers of magnets, motors and electronics increasingly need to document product classification, end users and shipment routes, and supply availability now depends on licences and geopolitics as much as on production capacity.
That environment tends to increase the value of processing capacity outside China. Rare earths such as neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium are essential for permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, defence systems and industrial automation.
Earlier this year, China also added several United States companies to its export control restricted list, including MP Materials, underscoring how quickly access to Chinese material can change.
Lynas's position in the market
Lynas is the world's largest producer of separated rare earths outside China. It mines at Mt Weld in Western Australia, processes material at Kalgoorlie and operates a separation plant in Malaysia, giving it an integrated chain from ore to oxide.
That footprint makes Lynas a reference point for governments and manufacturers seeking diversified supply. Alongside a small number of peers in the United States, it accounts for the bulk of commercial rare earth oxide supply produced beyond China's borders. That concentration means customer demand for non-China material tends to flow toward Lynas first, particularly when policy tension rises.
A profit rise that missed expectations
Last month, Lynas reported a sharp rise in annual profit, helped by record average realised prices for rare earth oxides and strong demand. Even so, the result fell short of market expectations, a reminder that cost pressures and production ramp-ups can blunt the benefit of higher prices. The market reaction showed that expectations for the company had risen alongside rare earth prices, leaving less room for operational slippage.
Higher prices for magnet materials have been a feature of the year, with tighter Chinese controls and strong demand from clean energy and electronics contributing to firmer pricing outside China.
Takeover talks that did not proceed
In early September, a Lynas spokesperson confirmed to Reuters that the company had been in takeover talks earlier in the year but that the discussions, which carried a high level of uncertainty, did not proceed.
The disclosure answered speculation rather than signalling a new process. However, it highlighted that strategic interest in Lynas exists, which is unsurprising given its scale and scarcity value as a non-China producer.
Any future approach would likely face scrutiny from Australian regulators, given the strategic nature of rare earths and the policy emphasis on domestic critical mineral processing.
Leadership search under way
Lynas is searching for a new leader following the retirement of its long-serving head, who guided the company through its expansion into Malaysia, Kalgoorlie and heavy rare earths separation.
The choice of successor will be closely watched. The incoming leader will inherit a business in the middle of expansion projects, a complex relationship with host governments and customers seeking long-term supply security. Continuity in customer relationships, especially with Japanese partners that have backed the company for many years, is likely to be a priority for the board during the search.
Sector context
Lynas is a member of the ASX 100 and remains the largest rare earths company on the local bourse by market value.
Readers following ASX Rare Earth Minerals will know that the sector has been busy this month. Developers are advancing refinery and mine projects, securing offtake agreements with automakers and wind turbine manufacturers, and lining up government-backed financing.
Chinese state players have also been moving to consolidate their position. Reporting this week noted that a Chinese state-owned rare earths group was in talks to acquire a company that owns an interest in MP Materials, adding to perceptions that the industry is increasingly shaped by strategic considerations.
Heavy rare earths are the pressure point
Much of the concern among Western manufacturers centres on heavy rare earths such as dysprosium and terbium, which improve the heat resistance of permanent magnets. China dominates separation of these elements, and supply outside China has been extremely limited.
Lynas has worked to build heavy rare earths separation capability in Malaysia, positioning it as among the few commercial sources of these materials outside China. Tighter enforcement of Chinese controls increases the attention on that capability from automakers, defence contractors and governments.
Heavy rare earths typically command much higher prices than light rare earths, so even modest volumes can make a meaningful contribution to revenue if pricing stays firm.
Government support across allied markets
Governments in Australia, the United States, Japan and Europe have stepped up support for rare earths supply chains through loans, grants, strategic reserves and offtake arrangements. Australia has used its export credit agency and critical minerals programs to back domestic refineries and mines.
For Lynas, this policy environment provides both opportunity and competition. Supportive policy can underpin customer demand and project financing, but it also accelerates the development of rival projects that may eventually add supply outside China.
Over time, the emergence of new producers in Australia, the United States and Brazil could erode some of the scarcity premium that Lynas currently enjoys, though most of those projects remain years from full production.
Pricing and demand drivers
Demand for magnet rare earths continues to be underpinned by electric vehicles, wind power, robotics and defence. Western customers are increasingly willing to sign long-term contracts with floor prices or index-linked pricing to secure non-China supply.
For Lynas, a combination of firm demand and supply restrictions from China supports pricing, although rare earth prices remain volatile and can move sharply on policy announcements or shifts in Chinese output quotas.
Leadership transition adds execution risk during a period of expansion, and the prospect of renewed corporate interest could introduce volatility in the share price. Currency movements also matter, as the company earns most of its revenue in United States dollars while reporting in Australian dollars.
What to watch next
Key signposts include the appointment of a new leader, the September quarter report and any further detail on expansion projects and customer agreements. The quarterly report will show whether production volumes and realised prices have continued to improve since the annual result.
Developments in Chinese export policy will continue to shape the sector's direction, and Lynas is likely to remain the primary listed barometer for how the market prices non-China rare earths supply. Its share price often moves with the wider sector on policy headlines, even when company-specific news is limited.

articles.title: Wunti Warns Against Repeating Oil Export Model With Critical Minerals - Business Post Nigeria
articles.summary: Wunti Warns Against Repeating Oil Export Model With Critical Minerals  Business Post Nigeria
articles.full_text:
By Adedapo Adesanya
Nigeria has been urged to move away from exporting unprocessed critical minerals and instead develop domestic processing and manufacturing value chains to avoid repeating the structural weaknesses created by its crude oil export model.
Speaking at the 2026 Concordia Annual Summit in New York, where he participated in a high-level panel on Rare Currency: Critical Minerals in a Shifting Global Economy, the chief executive of the World Energy Council Nigeria, Mr Bala Wunti, said Nigeria’s estimated 44 critical mineral types, including lithium, rare earth elements, nickel and cobalt, should become feedstock for domestic industrialisation rather than being exported in raw form.
Mr Wunti, a former Chief Upstream Investment Officer of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited, warned that exporting mineral concentrates and subsequently importing higher-value processed products would replicate the value leakage experienced in the petroleum sector.
“For half a century, Nigeria exported crude oil in its raw form and turned around to import refined petroleum products at astronomical costs. That structural anomaly created poverty, flight of capital, and economic vulnerability instead of wealth.
“We must not repeat that failure with lithium, tantalite, and rare earth elements,” Mr Wunti said.
The intervention comes as critical minerals gain strategic importance globally because of their role in batteries, renewable energy technologies, electric vehicles, advanced manufacturing and other industrial applications.
Mr Wunti identified the absence of standardised and bankable geological data as one of the principal constraints preventing large-scale institutional investment in Nigeria’s mining sector.
“The fundamental problem has been the gap between mineral potential and an investable project. Global investors do not deploy capital into potential; they deploy capital into bankable projects backed by JORC-compliant data.
“We had indications of minerals in the ground, but we lacked the commercial structuring needed to convince international financiers,” he said.
According to him, attracting serious private capital requires more than geological indications. Nigeria must provide reliable geological surveys, predictable regulatory frameworks, security for host communities, adequate power infrastructure and commercially viable routes to domestic and international markets.
Mr Wunti also identified the newly established Nigerian Solid Minerals Company (NSMC) as an important vehicle for addressing the bankability gap in the sector.
He said the company could help convert geological information and mineral discoveries into de-risked, commercially viable investment opportunities capable of attracting private capital.
For Nigeria, the strategic objective, he suggested, should therefore extend beyond increasing mineral production to building the infrastructure, processing capacity and industrial linkages required to capture a greater share of the value generated across the critical minerals supply chain.

What's the deal? The US and Australia have committed more than A$5 billion to Australian critical minerals projects under a joint framework agreed by President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. The programme targets nickel, cobalt, gallium, magnesium, vanadium, and graphite — materials needed for batteries, semiconductors, defence systems, and power grids.
Why now? A Reuters analysis dated September 14 shows how hard it is for Washington to loosen China's grip on processing. That has pushed Australia to the centre of Western supply-chain strategy.
China still dominates. According to International Energy Agency data cited by Reuters, China's share of global rare-earth refining slipped from about 90% in 2023 to roughly 85% in 2025. But its share of lithium, cobalt, and graphite processing has recently risen.
The long-term outlook is stark: even if every announced project outside China is built, the IEA estimates China could still control about 70% to 73% of global rare-earth refining in 2035.
How the deal grew. Trump and Albanese signed the "United States–Australia Framework for Securing of Supply in the Mining and Processing of Critical Minerals and Rare Earths" at the White House in October 2025. Each country initially agreed to commit at least $1 billion within six months, alongside a pipeline of priority projects worth about $8.5 billion.
In April 2026, the Australian government said the two countries would together provide more than A$5 billion to support Australian projects.
Who benefits? De.mem Limited is one company positioned for the investment cycle. It now earns nearly half its revenue in Western Australia, supplying the mining sector with water technology, pumps, specialty chemicals, and long-term services.
The signal: Raw material policy is becoming industrial and security policy. In February, US Vice President JD Vance proposed a preferential trade bloc for critical minerals to build supply chains with allied states — a sign that new mines alone won't close the gap, and that whole processing chains, not just deposits, are now the prize.

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Rare Earth Oxides (Nd/Pr Concentrates) market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global market for Rare Earth Oxides (Nd/Pr Concentrates) stands at a critical juncture, poised for transformative growth through 2035. As the indispensable feedstock for high-performance NdFeB permanent magnets, these concentrates are central to the global energy transition. The accelerating adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) and the rapid expansion of wind power capacity are the primary demand engines, with each EV traction motor and direct-drive wind turbine requiring substantial quantities of neodymium and praseodymium. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering historical data from 2012 to 2025.
It examines the intricate dynamics of supply and demand, trade flows, pricing mechanisms, and the competitive landscape. The market is characterized by a stark geographic concentration of supply, primarily in China, which presents significant risks and opportunities. The forecast period will witness a strategic push for supply chain diversification, increased recycling efforts, and technological innovations aimed at reducing rare earth intensity. This analysis is essential for manufacturers, investors, and policymakers navigating this strategically vital sector.
The baseline scenario for the Rare Earth Oxides (Nd/Pr Concentrates) market forecasts a robust compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.2% from 2026 to 2035, culminating in a market index of 220 (2025=100). This growth is underpinned by the irreversible momentum of the global energy transition. The primary demand driver is the permanent magnet sector, which consumes over 90% of Nd/Pr concentrates. Electric vehicle sales are projected to surge, with NdFeB magnets being critical for traction motors. Similarly, the wind energy sector, particularly offshore installations using direct-drive turbines, will require substantial volumes.
On the supply side, the market will continue to face tightness due to the long lead times for new mining and separation projects outside of China. This supply-demand imbalance is expected to keep prices elevated and volatile, incentivizing investments in recycling and alternative technologies. The baseline scenario assumes no major technological breakthroughs that would significantly reduce rare earth content in magnets, and a steady pace of policy support for clean energy. However, geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions remain key upside risks to prices and downside risks to availability.
The permanent magnet sector is the undisputed engine of Nd/Pr concentrate demand, accounting for over 90% of global consumption. This dominance is rooted in the superior magnetic properties of NdFeB magnets, which are essential for high-efficiency motors and generators. Currently, the automotive industry's shift to electric vehicles is the most powerful demand driver, as each EV traction motor requires approximately 1-2 kg of NdFeB magnets. Through 2035, this trend will accelerate, with EV sales projected to grow at a double-digit CAGR. Simultaneously, the wind energy sector, particularly offshore farms using direct-drive turbines, will consume significant volumes.
Demand-side indicators to watch include EV production volumes, wind capacity additions, and the average rare earth content per magnet. The sector's growth is also supported by miniaturization in electronics and the rise of robotics, which require compact, powerful magnets. However, potential thrifting and recycling could moderate the growth rate in the long term. Current trend: Strong growth driven by EV and wind energy.
Major trends: Shift towards heavy rare earth-free magnets to reduce dependency on dysprosium and terbium, Increasing use of grain boundary diffusion to enhance magnet performance with less rare earth content, Growth in recycling of end-of-life magnets to recover Nd/Pr, Development of alternative motor designs that require less or no rare earths, and Expansion of magnet production capacity outside China to secure supply chains.
Representative participants: China Northern Rare Earth (Group) High-Tech Co., Ltd, Lynas Rare Earths Ltd, MP Materials Corp, Neo Performance Materials Inc, Vacuumschmelze GmbH & Co. KG, and Shin-Etsu Chemical Co., Ltd.
The catalysts sector represents a smaller but stable demand stream for Nd/Pr concentrates, primarily in fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) for petroleum refining and in automotive catalytic converters. Neodymium and praseodymium oxides are used to enhance the thermal stability and oxygen storage capacity of catalyst materials. Currently, demand is driven by global fuel production and tightening emissions regulations, particularly in emerging economies. Through 2035, the growth in this sector will be moderate, as the rise of electric vehicles may reduce demand for automotive catalysts in developed markets, but this will be offset by increased refining activity in Asia and the Middle East.
Demand-side indicators include refinery throughput, vehicle production, and emission standards. The sector is also exploring new applications in chemical synthesis and environmental catalysis, which could provide additional upside. However, the overall share of Nd/Pr concentrates in catalysts is expected to remain relatively small compared to permanent magnets. Current trend: Steady growth in petroleum refining and automotive catalysts.
Major trends: Increasing demand for cleaner fuels driving catalyst innovation, Shift towards electric vehicles reducing automotive catalyst demand in some regions, Growth in refining capacity in Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, Development of rare earth-based catalysts for chemical recycling, and Stringent emission regulations boosting catalyst loadings.
Representative participants: BASF SE, Albemarle Corporation, W.R. Grace & Co, Johnson Matthey Plc, and Haldor Topsoe A/S.
Polishing powders, primarily cerium oxide-based, are a traditional application for rare earth oxides, but Nd/Pr concentrates are used in some specialized polishing formulations for high-precision optics and electronics. The demand story here is one of steady, niche growth. Currently, the sector is supported by the booming consumer electronics industry, where rare earth polishing powders are used to finish glass screens, semiconductor wafers, and optical lenses. Through 2035, demand will be driven by the increasing complexity of electronic devices and the growth of precision manufacturing. Demand-side indicators include semiconductor wafer production, flat panel display output, and smartphone shipments.
However, the use of Nd/Pr in polishing is relatively small and faces competition from other materials. The trend towards miniaturization and higher precision will require advanced polishing solutions, potentially benefiting Nd/Pr-based products. Recycling of polishing slurries is also gaining traction, which could affect primary demand. Current trend: Moderate growth driven by electronics and optics.
Major trends: Growing demand for high-precision optics in electronics and medical devices, Increasing use of chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) in semiconductor manufacturing, Development of eco-friendly polishing slurries with reduced rare earth content, Recycling of polishing waste to recover rare earths, and Shift towards alternative polishing materials like diamond and silica.
Representative participants: Solvay S.A, Ferro Corporation, Cabot Microelectronics Corporation, Asahi Glass Co., Ltd, and Showa Denko K.K.
Rare earth oxides, including Nd/Pr concentrates, are used as glass additives to impart specific optical properties, such as color correction and UV absorption. Neodymium oxide is particularly valued for its ability to filter yellow light, making it useful in welding goggles and specialty lenses. The demand story for this sector is one of stability rather than rapid growth. Currently, the market is driven by niche applications in protective eyewear, architectural glass, and automotive glass. Through 2035, demand will be supported by the increasing use of smart glass and advanced coatings, but overall growth will be modest. Demand-side indicators include construction activity, automotive production, and safety equipment demand.
The sector faces competition from alternative materials and technologies, but the unique optical properties of Nd/Pr oxides ensure a persistent, albeit small, market. Recycling of glass containing rare earths is not yet widespread, so primary demand will continue. Current trend: Stable demand from specialty glass applications.
Major trends: Growing demand for energy-efficient architectural glass, Increasing use of rare earths in smart glass and electrochromic windows, Development of rare earth-free glass additives for cost reduction, Expansion of automotive glass applications with advanced coatings, and Rising safety standards driving demand for protective eyewear.
Representative participants: Corning Incorporated, Saint-Gobain S.A, Asahi Glass Co., Ltd, Nippon Sheet Glass Co., Ltd, and Guardian Industries Corp.
The ceramics sector represents a small but diverse outlet for Nd/Pr concentrates, used in both traditional ceramics for coloring and in advanced ceramics for electronic and structural applications. Neodymium and praseodymium oxides are used to produce vibrant colors in glazes and to enhance the properties of advanced ceramic materials like zirconia. Currently, demand is driven by the construction and electronics industries. Through 2035, growth will be slow, as traditional ceramics face competition from other materials, but advanced ceramics in electronics, aerospace, and medical implants will offer opportunities. Vancouver, British Columbia--(Newsfile Corp. - September 28, 2026) - Zodiac Gold Inc. (TSXV: ZAU) (OTCQB: ZAUIF) (FSE: K19) ("Zodiac Gold" or the "Company"), a West African gold exploration company, is pleased to report that it has completed a soil geochemical survey (the "Soil Sampling Program") across an area of 530 km2 that has identified gold, nickel, cobalt, chromium and copper anomalies within the Company's licenses covering 2,316 km². These results are consistent with a national stream sediment survey conducted by Liberia's Ministry of Mines and Energy through the Chinese Geological Survey and may indicate potential for a polymetallic mineral system as well as pointing to underlying mafic lithologies which are highly prospective for gold throughout the region.
Program Highlights
- Analysis of national maps showing interpolated anomalous zones based on stream sediment sample point data, shows that stream sediment samples in Zodiac Gold's license package are in the top 0.5% of the most anomalous areas of the national dataset for sixteen elements. 
  - These elements are chromium, cobalt, lanthanum, lead, lithium, manganese, nickel, niobium, samarium, silver, tantalum, tin, uranium, vanadium, zinc and zirconium.
  - Every one of these elements is designated a critical mineral on the U.S. Geological Survey's 2025 List of Critical Minerals.
  - Chromium in particular is a strategic input for stainless steel and defense superalloys, while nickel and cobalt are core battery-supply-chain metals - end-uses at the centre of United States and allied efforts to secure non-Chinese sources of these materials.
- 10,661-sample survey covering 530 km² of the Bomi South and Bong West licenses, with a line spacing of 500 m and sample stations every 100 m along each line. Laboratory gold assays have been received for 9,160 samples and 2,270 samples have been scanned to date using a portable X-ray fluorescence ("pXRF") unit to provide multielement data. Additional results will be announced as more data becomes available.
- Results show coincident gold and arsenic anomalism in discrete east-west trending zones across the sampled area, with individual anomalies up to 2.5 km in length (Figure 1). Another zone shows gold anomalism (results up to 1.16 g/t Au) in close proximity to a northwest trending Todi Shear Zone structure. Previously unknown artisanal workings have been identified and lithologies interpreted from airborne magnetic data along this trend, to be followed up on the ground, include possible itabirite +/- mafic / ultramafic greenstone units, granitized greenstone and mafic amphibolite.
- Multielement pXRF data across 45 elements is being evaluated for gold pathfinders and critical minerals, and has been benchmarked against the 616-sample national stream sediment survey (Figures 2 and 3): 
  - Nickel: Peak stream sediment result in the top 0.5% of the national survey. Peak pXRF soil value of 686 ppm, with nickel rising in step with chromium.
  - Cobalt: Peak stream sediment result in the top 0.5% of the national survey. Peak pXRF soil value of 894 ppm.
  - Chromium: Peak stream sediment result in the top 0.5% of the national survey. Peak pXRF soil value of 3,368 ppm, with 14 samples above 1,000 ppm concentrated in two clusters.
  - Copper: Parts of the license lie within the highest class of the national survey. Peak pXRF soil value of 512 ppm.
  - Rare earth elements: detectable rare earth elements including cerium (to 253 ppm), lanthanum (to 176 ppm) and yttrium (to 63 ppm), as well as more isolated neodymium and praseodymium anomalism (to +200 ppm). Note that the peak rare earth stream sediment areas have not yet been sampled.
  - Additional critical minerals: vanadium to 709 ppm, niobium to 61 ppm, barium to 3,002 ppm, zinc to 200 ppm, lead to 167 ppm, manganese to 2,291 ppm.
"The Soil Sampling Program is additional support for our belief in the high prospectivity of our district-scale land package, not only for gold but also potentially for critical minerals and iron ore. The Ministry's national survey data first pointed us to the critical minerals potential across this license package. What our own soil sampling and pXRF program has now confirmed is that those indications are real, they are coherent over multiple kilometres and in several elements," said David Kol, CEO of Zodiac Gold. "Combined with the gold pathfinder trend we're seeing in arsenic, this tells us we could be sitting on more than one mineralizing system within a single license block."
Mr Kol continued: "Gold remains the Company's top priority, however, the critical minerals signature within the license package may be a significant additional opportunity. This aligns directly with the priority now shared across the United States and its G7 allies of securing diversified, reliable supplies of critical minerals from trusted partner jurisdictions and reducing dependence on a single dominant supplier. Liberia - a longstanding United States partner with a U.S.-dollar-based economy, an English-speaking, common-law business environment and deep historical ties to the United States - is well positioned to contribute to these allied supply chains. Nickel, cobalt, chromium and copper, the elements most strongly expressed in the Company's soil data, are all U.S.-designated critical minerals. Realizing this potential will be subject to successful follow-up exploration and studies of priority targets."
Technical Significance
Arsenic is a well-established pathfinder for orogenic gold and the Company considers this trend a high-priority target for follow-up. The coincident nickel-cobalt-chromium enrichment pattern is typically associated with mafic-to-ultramafic rocks. These lithologies are highly prospective for gold throughout the region and may also be prospective for laterite-hosted nickel-cobalt mineralization, magmatic nickel-copper-cobalt sulfide mineralization or chromite, all important sources of the battery and critical minerals feedstocks currently sought by North American and allied supply chains.
Interpretation of regional geophysical data shows potential intrusions and granitized greenstone belt which could have exploration potential for critical minerals and rare earths. These initial interpretations will be refined as additional results become available and field mapping is completed.

Planned soil sample locations were navigated to using a handheld GPS. On arrival, each site was assessed for potential sources of contamination and moved if necessary, and the actual location coordinates were recorded. Details such as land use, slope angle and direction, soil type, soil color, moisture content and depth of sample were recorded. A 50-60 cm hole was dug and approximately 2-3 kg of material from the bottom of the hole was placed in a plastic bag labeled with the sample number. Where it was not possible to dig to a depth of 50-60 cm, the sample was taken from as deep as possible and the actual depth was recorded. Equipment was cleaned between samples to avoid contamination.

Where necessary, clumps of material were broken down carefully using a pestle before sieving. articles.title: European critical minerals projects face funding crunch as strategic status fails to prevent bankruptcies - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: European critical minerals projects face funding crunch as strategic status fails to prevent bankruptcies  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
Strategic Ambitions Meet Financial Reality
Mining and refining companies across the European Union are demanding a dedicated budget for critical raw materials, warning that strategic project status under the bloc's landmark 2024 law has not translated into accessible financing.
The push for a specific budget line follows the high-profile collapse of Viridian Lithium, a French refinery designated as a strategic project, and a joint warning from nearly half of the EU's recognized strategic mineral projects citing acute liquidity shortages.
Under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), which came into force in May 2024, the EU set ambitious targets to secure its supply chains for the green and digital transitions. By 2030, the bloc aims to extract at least 10 percent of its annual consumption of critical materials domestically, process 40 percent, and recycle 25 percent, while ensuring no more than 65 percent of any strategic raw material comes from a single third country.
To achieve these goals, the European Commission selected 60 strategic projects across the value chain. However, the legislation did not include a dedicated funding mechanism, leaving developers to compete for existing EU financial instruments and national state aid.
Liquidity Warnings and High-Profile Collapse
The fragility of this approach was exposed in March 2026 when Viridian Lithium, a Strasbourg-based startup planning a major lithium refining facility in Alsace, was placed into judicial liquidation. Despite being recognized under the CRMA framework, the company succumbed to what industry observers describe as unfulfilled investment promises and severe market pressures.
The bankruptcy sent shockwaves through the sector, highlighting the gap between regulatory fast-tracking and actual capital deployment. In August, representatives from 23 of the 60 designated strategic projects wrote to the European Commission, warning of "acute liquidity problems and market pressures" that threaten their viability.
During a subsequent meeting with Commission officials, project promoters complained about the inefficiency of current mineral financing structures and the lack of a reliable, predictable market for their future production, according to documents reviewed by EUobserver. The companies argue that without ring-fenced capital, critical minerals will continue to lose out to other political and economic priorities within the broader EU budget.
Commission Defends Existing Frameworks
The European Commission has pushed back against calls for a new budget line. Following a meeting of EU industry ministers, Stefan Séjourné, the Vice-President for Industrial Strategy, stated that the bloc is accelerating both financing and administrative procedures.
The Commission maintains it has established a framework capable of mobilizing €1.7 billion through existing programs like the Innovation Fund. However, industry stakeholders counter that accessing these funds remains notoriously difficult, burdened by complex application processes that do not align with the capital-intensive realities of mining.
When pressed on the industry's demands, an EU official told EUobserver that no dedicated fund would be created. The official noted that financing from the next multiannual budget will instead reflect "established needs for flexibility, predictability and efficiency," suggesting CRMA projects must integrate into broader industrial funding streams.
Global Competition and Market Volatility
The urgency of the EU's domestic ambitions is magnified by intense global competition for critical minerals. Nations with established mining sectors and state-backed financing have moved aggressively to secure supply chains, often driving down global prices through overcapacity.
This market volatility severely impacts European startups, which struggle to secure private investment when global commodity prices fluctuate wildly. The CRMA identifies 17 strategic raw materials, including lithium, nickel, cobalt, and rare earth elements, as vital for the bloc's economic security. However, the capital expenditure required to build refineries in Europe, coupled with stringent regulations, makes domestic production inherently more expensive than importing processed materials.
Industry advocates argue that without direct financial intervention, European projects will remain uncompetitive. The failure of the French refinery demonstrates that strategic status does not shield companies from fundamental market economics or the high cost of capital in Europe.
The Geopolitical Stakes of Supply Chain Sovereignty
The funding dispute underscores a central tension in the EU's industrial policy: the desire for strategic autonomy versus the financial constraints of a fragmented capital market. The CRMA was designed to reduce Europe's heavy reliance on single third countries for the processing of vital minerals essential for electric vehicles and advanced electronics.
Yet, the collapse of Viridian Lithium suggests that regulatory designation alone is insufficient to de-risk investments. Environmental and community groups have also challenged some projects, with lawsuits filed against strategic designations that allegedly bypassed sufficient environmental assessments.
As the EU attempts to build a domestic critical raw materials ecosystem, the coming months will test whether the Commission's mobilization framework can be deployed quickly enough to prevent further insolvencies. For the strategic projects, accelerated permits mean little without the capital required to break ground.

articles.title: Ex-China heavy rare earths continue to surge: Q3 2026 Rare Earths Price Review - Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.summary: Ex-China heavy rare earths continue to surge: Q3 2026 Rare Earths Price Review  Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.full_text:
Light and heavy rare earth prices diverged sharply for much of Q3 2026. The BMI Praseodymium-Neodymium Oxide (PrNd) DDP China price eased by just 1% over the period, while the BMI PrNd CIF North America and Europe prices fell more sharply, slipping below the $110/kg floor built into MP Materials and Lynas Rare Earths' agreements with the US Department of Defense. In contrast, ex-China dysprosium, terbium and yttrium prices surged, with BMI Dysprosium Oxide CIF Europe increasing 150% by quarter-end.
The defining theme of Q3 was the extreme widening of the China–ex-China bifurcation within heavy rare earths, a dynamic Benchmark's forecasting team expects to persist, noting that the ex-China DyTb premium is still the economic signal required to bring new heavy rare earth capacity online.
“There is mounting evidence that ex-China heavy rare earth supply chains remain acutely under-supplied relative to demand, a dynamic reflected in pricing across the quarter,” said George Ingall, a senior rare earth price analyst at Benchmark. “Chinese export restrictions continued to constrain availability, with buyers paying significant premiums to secure larger volumes of dysprosium and terbium. Light rare earths beyond China remained oversupplied, though this dynamic is stabilising.”
How wide did heavy rare earth price bifurcation get in Q3?
CIF Europe dysprosium oxide prices are now around 16.3 times DDP China price levels, up from 6.8 times at the end of Q2. This is even starker for yttrium oxide, for which the CIF North America price sits at roughly 196 times the equivalent DDP China price.
Over the course of July, dysprosium oxide CIF Europe prices climbed more than 16% as ex-China buyers scrambled for scarce material, while the Chinese domestic assessment moved only fractionally. Terbium oxide in China rose nearly 6% on tight availability, while yttrium markets were comparatively subdued in both regions.
In August, ex-China heavy rare earths rose, with dysprosium oxide CIF Europe surging more than 32%, terbium oxide CIF Europe by 10%, and yttrium oxide CIF North America nearly 18%. Scarcity continued to underpin heavy rare earth pricing. A US presidential determination moved to treat recoverable rare earths and end-of-life magnets as strategic defence resources, a step that could improve future domestic access to secondary dysprosium and terbium feedstock. Chinese domestic heavy rare earth pricing was comparatively muted in August, with dysprosium and terbium easing slightly.
By September, dysprosium oxide CIF Europe gained 56% to reach an average of $3,500/kg and terbium oxide rose 23% to $6,745/kg, driven by premiums on larger-volume transactions, while Chinese domestic dysprosium and terbium prices continued to retreat from their mid-Q3 highs. Yttrium oxide held steady in both China and North America, with ongoing US production limiting further upward momentum.
What happened to PrNd oxide prices in Q3?
In July, PrNd CIF Europe/North America pricing held flat, while prices in China ticked modestly higher before renewed weakness took hold. Then, in August, ex-China PrNd oxide prices fell over 13%, with the decline accelerating late in the month as ex-China producers, wary of the reputational sensitivity of selling into China, redirected volume toward an increasingly oversupplied ex-China market. This led to a 7.3% drop between 6–20 August alone. Chinese domestic PrNd, now commanding a premium, fell a more moderate 5% over the same month.
PrNd prices stabilised in China by September, with the oxide assessment edging up 1% to an average of RMB729,500/t (USD$108,696), while ex-China prices rose 12% to $106,500/t on a CIF basis.
What could impact rare earths prices in Q4?
An update is due from China’s government on rare earth export restrictions when the current controls expire in November.
“Buyers speaking to Benchmark have already indicated they have had little luck exporting ytterbium and erbium from China in recent months, even though these minerals are not currently under export controls,” Ingall said. “In North America and Europe, meanwhile, demo- and pilot-scale procurement from aspiring magnet makers is likely to drive up heavy rare earth oxide prices.”

articles.title: Critical Minerals: 5 Smart Bets in a Powerful New Race - globalbrandsmagazine.com
articles.summary: Critical Minerals: 5 Smart Bets in a Powerful New Race  globalbrandsmagazine.com
articles.full_text:
Every electric car, wind turbine, data centre and smartphone rests on a short list of raw materials that most people never think about. Critical minerals, the group that includes lithium, copper, cobalt, nickel, graphite and the rare earths, have quietly become some of the most strategically important commodities on the planet. In 2026 the race to secure them has moved from mining conferences into corporate boardrooms.
The reason is demand. According to the International Energy Agency, lithium demand is projected to rise roughly 353% between 2024 and 2040, while graphite demand could climb about 131%. Global battery demand alone grew more than 35% in 2025, passing 1.5 terawatt-hours, with grid-scale storage joining electric vehicles as a major pull. These are not niche materials any more. They are the building blocks of the electrified economy.
Why critical minerals matter now
The shift is being driven by three overlapping trends. Electric vehicles need large batteries, and batteries need lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite. Electricity grids are expanding and modernising, which takes enormous quantities of copper. And the motors, magnets and electronics inside everything from wind turbines to robots depend on rare earth elements. Add fast-growing demand for computing power, and the pressure on supply only builds.
For companies, that turns raw materials into a competitive issue. A carmaker without secure battery materials cannot promise buyers a steady supply. An electronics firm exposed to a single source of rare earths carries a risk it may not fully understand. What used to be a purchasing detail is now a question of corporate resilience.
A concentrated supply chain
The awkward truth about critical minerals is that supply is heavily concentrated, especially in the refining stage where raw ore becomes usable material. The IEA notes that for copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths, the combined market share of the top three refining nations rose to about 86% in 2024, up from around 82% in 2020. Battery recycling capacity is even more concentrated, with one country accounting for roughly 90% of material recovery capacity.
| Mineral | Projected demand growth (2024-2040) | 
|---|---|
| Lithium | ~+353% | 
| Graphite | ~+131% | 
| Copper, nickel, rare earths | Strong, steady growth | 
| Global battery demand (2025) | +35% year on year, past 1.5 TWh | 
Concentration is not a moral judgement, it is a business risk. When most of the world’s refining or recycling sits in a few places, a single disruption, whether weather, technical or logistical, can ripple through every industry that depends on the output. That is why diversification has become a strategic priority for so many companies at once.
The companies that treat critical minerals as an afterthought today are the ones most likely to be caught short tomorrow.
The recycling opportunity
One of the most promising responses is recycling. Today, average recycling rates across key energy minerals sit at roughly 10%, but the IEA expects that to climb towards 20% by 2040 under current policies, with cobalt and copper further ahead. Recovering minerals from used batteries and scrap could become a meaningful second source of supply, and a business in its own right, though it needs sustained investment in collection and processing to reach its potential.
The scale of investment required is large. Diversifying magnet rare earth supply chains alone would take around $60 billion over the next decade, by IEA estimates. That is capital looking for a return, which is exactly why miners, manufacturers and investors are circling the sector.
Recycling has a second benefit beyond supply. Recovering critical minerals from old devices and batteries uses far less energy and water than digging fresh ore, which appeals to companies under pressure to shrink their environmental footprint. It also keeps valuable material inside the economies that already own it, rather than shipping it out as waste and buying it back later as finished product. For brands that want a supply story they can stand behind, a credible recycling loop is becoming a genuine advantage.
Copper, the quiet giant
Lithium and rare earths grab the headlines, but copper may be the most important critical mineral of all, because almost nothing electrifies without it. Every electric car, charging point, solar farm, wind turbine and data centre needs large amounts of copper wiring, and demand keeps climbing as grids expand to carry more power. Unlike some exotic materials, copper is mined and used at massive scale, which makes even small imbalances between supply and demand ripple widely through prices.
New copper mines take a long time to bring online, often a decade or more from discovery to production. That lag is exactly why analysts worry about a squeeze later this decade, as demand from electrification and computing runs ahead of new supply. For companies planning long-lived investments, from carmakers to utilities, copper is no longer something to take for granted. It is a strategic input to be secured well in advance.
The same pattern shows up across the group. Building a new mine, refinery or recycling plant is slow and capital-intensive, while demand can shift quickly. That mismatch between fast demand and slow supply is the core tension in critical minerals, and it is why the topic has jumped up the corporate agenda rather than staying in the commodities pages.
How companies are securing critical minerals
The corporate playbook is taking shape. Manufacturers are signing long-term offtake deals directly with miners, sometimes years before a mine opens, to lock in supply. Some are investing in mining and refining projects themselves rather than relying on the open market. Others are building recycling operations to create a domestic loop. And a wave of consolidation is under way, as shown by high-profile talks such as those we covered between Glencore and Rio Tinto.
Investment is following the demand. Mining and refining projects that struggled to raise money a few years ago are attracting fresh capital, and specialist funds have sprung up to back critical minerals ventures from exploration through to recycling. Governments and large manufacturers are co-investing too, sharing the risk of building supply that may take years to come good. For patient investors, the appeal is a rare combination of structural demand growth and genuine scarcity, though the sector carries real risks around cost overruns, permitting and price swings.
The corporate lesson is to map exposure before it becomes a crisis. That means knowing which critical minerals sit inside your products, where they are refined, and what would happen if a single source went offline. Firms that can answer those questions calmly are in a far stronger position than those discovering the answer during a shortage. Increasingly, that mapping is being done at board level, alongside the traditional risks of currency, cyber and demand.
The through-line connects to stories GBM has followed elsewhere, from the race to commercialise solid-state batteries to the business of carbon capture and the wider return of hardware. All of them depend, in the end, on getting enough of the right materials at a price that works. Critical minerals have become the quiet foundation of the next industrial era, and the companies treating them as a strategic priority are the ones building on solid ground. For more, see our reports and insights coverage.
